Hey, could you quickly explain to me why you are talking about DirectX drawing? In our renderer, we're not using DirectX, right? We're using Vulkan or Metal. I actually don't quite understand why you talk about DirectX failures.
Is that generally the case that Windows doesn't have broken, or why is it like this yet?

Right, I understand. Let's just make sure we don't want to specialise on direct 3D. Hopefully, our code can stay mostly just expecting Vulkan. If we have to, in this case, use direct 3D, get a minimum fix in so it works, just so people who actually also have the same situation can still run the game. But it's not our goal.

Did we implement this for the UI? I said earlier that there was this kind of issue where sometimes the text would appear before the background, or the text would slightly adjust in position, like a frame, after the UI first showed. I was asking for these kinds of things to be automatically done.

I'm wondering if you already meant to do that and how you implemented it, because the way I think would probably be best is if all elements that concern a UI are basically part of a group. Only when the group flag, the ready flag, becomes true, you start rendering it, and before that, you just ignore it. This, to me, sounds like a very GPU-friendly way of doing it.

Just to make sure, "ready here" doesn't mean all sprites are loaded. "Ready here" means we have sent all information for rendering this UI to the GPU. This way, we basically ensure that everything starts rendering in the same frame. The reason why this should not include whether all sprites are loaded is because if a single sprite is not loaded, the whole UI just doesn't show at all. That's no go for user experience.
I want to make this clear again: in general, we do not want to do any rendering on the CPU. Everything has to happen in shaders on the GPU, and shaders that are written to be efficient.

Also, another thing is I have noticed, in general, that quite often we have low frame rates. It would be great if the framework counter has a second option added that not only shows the milliseconds but also shows:
- the milliseconds spent on the CPU
- the milliseconds spent on the GPU
- how long the GPU has just spent waiting for the CPU


Also, because of this in general, I think you should do a review to check how often we synchronise between the CPU and the GPU, because optimally we don't want to synchronise at all. The GPU should just run, and we just upload data, and we never actually synchronise. The only thing we do is we send control codes that become active on a specific frame. For example, if we change map position, then this update only applies at frame X. If we have a partially rendered image, we don't get screen tearing from concurrent updates.

Regarding how we can make sure that data doesn't change halfway through, probably the easiest way to do this is to have three buffers:
- the buffer that's currently rendering
- the buffer that is going to render next
- the in-preparation buffer


We have an extra field that is a pointer between the last two of these. When the game wants to update, it takes this pointer and looks at which of the two is the current working scratch. It puts all data there, and once it's done, it flips over the pointer from the current next frame thing to the now-prepared new data.

What the GPU is doing is rendering a whole frame. When the whole frame is done, it doesn't copy over. It actually switches the pointer from what is currently the next frame to what is currently the next frame. It switches those pointers out atomically.

Now, the next atomic update would be the CPU switching it over to the previous render frame. This way, we never have these inconsistencies because both the GPU and CPU coordinate only via this pointer and these three memory areas that have the control in them.

The important bit here is that we don't want to have the whole world and everything uploaded three times. Only really control data, like camera position and an active UI pointer or something like that, is what's uploaded in this control area, so it's a very small amount of data, not a lot.
What do you mean by software renderers? We don't have a software renderer. We only have a GPU renderer, right?

All right, my question is then: why is there a 150-second wait in there? Is that the software renderer's code, or is that our own code? If it's our own code, why do we need to specialise our code for the software renderer? If it's a direct 3D renderer, right, it can still just process our shaders. Most of the other code was written for the W GPU and is generic, so I don't understand why we have to specialise at all here.

Well, regarding the cursor, whenever the cursor is not captured, the main cursor is just the normal operating system cursor with our icon set. The operating system is rendering the cursor, not the game. This is the way we make the cursor be frame-independent. Even if frames temporarily get low, we avoid lag. Of course, these cursor updates then cannot wait on the other GPU code. The way you have to do it is that they just have to run in a different thread from all the other code.

You do have a macOS VM, right? The only difference is that it's arch, but having the single-process dual stack is just the same on the x64 macOS VM, so you should be able to test it. Yeah, sure, it doesn't have a GPU, I guess, but I believe you could give it 3D acceleration by passing it from the AMD integrated GPU, using it as a source for a GPU-accelerated add-on for the VM, right?
Did you finish everything? If not, please continue till everything is done. Yes and no, the MacBook Neo is still offline. Test everything in different ways. Be creative.

Also, remember that we did have the performance goal when we ran on the iGPU AMD in 4K. We want to have 240 frames per second. This is also something we need to verify and make sure this actually happens, because to achieve that goal, we will very likely find a lot of remaining footguns: stupid code that creates arbitrary delays or locks that should be removed and fixed.
